issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Grief Reminders' is not well aligned with the indexed trauma of witnessing domestic violence in childhood unless there was also a salient bereavement/loss component. None of the other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal items indicate traumatic loss, so this strategy appears to target a different problem domain than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is hard to reconcile with this patient's age (21), single status, and the rest of the profile unless a specific caretaking or protective role is central to the trauma narrative. The other items emphasize danger sensitivity, helpless coping, and injustice toward perpetrators, but do not support a salient role-failure theme, making this appraisal feel insufficiently grounded in the profile.

vignette:
Valentina is a 21-year-old Salvadoran-American animator, currently single, who presented for her initial intake reporting a PCL-5 score of 39. She grew up in a household where her father's violence toward her mother was a recurring feature of her childhood - not rare or exceptional, but woven into the ordinary texture of evenings and weekends. What she remembers most viscerally is not any single incident but a composite that her mind has fused into something almost cinematic: the sound of something heavy striking a wall, the particular smell of her father's cologne mixed with cigarette smoke, and the sight of a framed family photograph knocked from the shelf and left face-down on the floor. No one was ever held responsible. Her father left when she was twelve and, as far as Valentina knows, has faced no legal or social consequence for what he did. She has come to believe, with a quiet and absolute certainty, that the people who cause harm simply do not pay for it.

Valentina works as a junior animator at a small studio, and it is there that the past most reliably finds her. Her workspace is visually dense - reference photos pinned to corkboards, stills from productions tacked above monitors - and on more than one occasion a colleague's photograph of a domestic interior, or a still featuring a certain kind of lighting, has stopped her cold. When such images appear, the memory does not arrive gradually; it surfaces with a vividness she describes as more real than anything she actually lived yesterday, accompanied sometimes by the ghost of that cologne, a sensory intrusion that feels to her like evidence that the past is not past. These triggers pull the memory forward with such force that she finds herself scanning the studio for exits, her body already on alert before her mind has caught up. Unexpected movement in her peripheral vision - a colleague reaching past her, a door swinging open - produces a physical startle response she cannot suppress, and she has grown chronically watchful in a way that exhausts her. She is frequently irritable at work, and there have been two incidents of sharp, disproportionate anger at colleagues, one of which her supervisor noted in a performance review.

Because the memory arrives with such intensity, Valentina has developed the habit of pushing it away before it can complete itself - she describes a kind of internal flinching, a refusal to let the scene finish. But this suppression, rather than emptying the memory, seems to keep it pressurised, so that it breaks through again more readily the next time a trigger appears. The hypervigilance that the triggers produce also keeps her in a state of low-grade arousal that makes the memory more accessible, not less - she is always, in some sense, already listening for the sound of something thrown.

Her avoidance has taken on several forms over the past year. She avoids anything that reminds her of her father - certain names, certain physical types, certain music - and she has stopped making plans for the future, as though committing to a future state would be a form of hubris the world would punish. She controls her eating strictly, measuring portions and refusing spontaneity around food; she experiences this as the one domain in which she holds genuine authority, though the rigidity of it has begun to isolate her socially, making shared meals with friends difficult. These strategies, she knows on some level, are not working: the avoidance keeps the memory unprocessed and raw, so that when something slips through her defences, the response is all the more acute, feeding back into the hypervigilance she is trying to manage.

What frightens Valentina most is her own sense of fragility - she is convinced she cannot manage even minor stressors, that the slightest disruption will undo her. She is haunted by the feeling that she is helpless against whatever comes next. What finally brought her to seek help was the performance review, which she experienced not as a professional setback but as confirmation of everything she already feared about herself. What she is most hoping for, she said quietly at the end of the intake, is to feel like the past is somewhere she has actually left.
